title: Back-stress-induced strengthening and strain hardening in dual-phase steel
abstract: Strain hardening for ductility remains challenging especially at high yield strength when dislocation plasticity is usually invalid. The hetero-deformation provides an effective route to induce extra back stress hardening specifically in hetero-structures inherently with large mismatch of mechanical responses, e.g. flow stress and strain hardening etc., upon applied loading. In this paper, both strengthening and strain hardening were investigated in a dual- phase steel, consisting of ductile γ-austenite and almost non-deformable B2 intermetallic phase as the second phase of volume fraction of 23%. The chemical composition was 0.86C, 16Mn, 10Al, 5Ni, balance Fe (wt.%). Of special note is two distinct hetero-deformation responses during both tensile and interrupted unload-reload testing. One is the yield-drop, while the other is hysteresis loop. Both unceasingly appear even from the elasto-plastic yield stage up to whole uniform deformation. The measured back stress and resultant back stress hardening account for a large proportion of global flow stress and strain hardening. Further, both Schmid factor and Kernel average misorientation (KAM) values were measured after tensile deformation. Un-expected, only γ-grains bordering on B2-phase show a significant decrease in the average Schmid factor, relative to almost unchanged in left γ-grains still next to γ-ones as well as B2-phase. This indicates that γ-grains adjacent to B2-phase bear the vast majority of plastic strains, not simple strain partitioning between γ and B2. Because of this, from the onset of yielding to end of tensile deformation, those γ-grains, in contrast to left γ-grains and B2 phase, exhibit a maximal increment in KAM values. This serves as a solid evidence of the generation of geometrically necessary dislocations to accommodate strain gradient near γ/B2 phase boundaries. It turns out that hetero-deformation due to plastic incompatibility induces the operation of back stresses, leading to both strengthening and strain hardening as well. Finally, a microstructure-based model was developed to calculate back stress which was well consistent with experimentally measured back stress.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Both strength and ductility are two critical mechanical properties of metallic materials. However, ductility, i.e. uniform elongation during tensile loading, becomes disappointedly low especially when yield strength increases significantly  [1–5] . This is due mainly to the shortage of strain hardening in either the severely cold-worked or grain-refined micro-structures which almost nullify traditional dislocation plasticity  [1,3,6] . So far, the strategies of two kinds are developed to enhance strain hardening. The first is to promote the storage of dislocations to recover intra-granular dislocation plasticity for forest hardening, e.g. nano-twinned grains  [7] , nano-precipitation  [8,9] , and grain refinement  [10]  etc. The second is to introduce the hetero-deformation-induced hardening mainly via trans-scale hetero-structuring of varying kinds for long-range inter-granular back stress hardening  [11–13]  and strain de-localization  [14] .

Recently, great interest has been aroused in hetero-structures (HS) of metallic materials  [11–27] . HSs usually feature either a trans-scale microarchitecture in terms of grain sizes, e.g. gradient structure  [14–16,23] , lamellar structure  [11,19,20,27] , hetero-geneous grain structure in a single-phase structure  [11] , and dual- and multi-phase microstructure  [23–27] . Therein, vast mismatch of plastic responses inevitably exists upon loading  [12,13] , such as yield strength, flow stress, and strain hardenability etc. For example, strong nano-sized grains of hardly any ductility are in sharp contrast with soft coarse-grains of large ductility  [11] . During plastic deformation, plastic incompatibility occurs mainly at either the grain boundaries or phase boundaries, leading to the presence of strain gradient across boundaries  [12–15,28–31] . The geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) are thus necessary to form near these boundaries to provide compatible deformation  [28–31] . Further, these GNDs also pile up and interact with varying boundaries, triggering the inter-granular back stress which plays a crucial role in work hardening  [12–15,30] . Just because of this, HSs will harvest sustainable strain hardening and resultant ductility, even comparable to that in their coarse-grained counterparts  [11,15,17,24–26] . Further, yielding in HS is undoubtedly elasto-plastic co-deformation due to large contrast of yield strength among either trans-scale grains or multi-phases  [12,13] . The introduction of GNDs may also lead to an extra strengthening effect as reported in a grain-size gradient structure  [12,13,16,32] .

The dual-phase and multi-phase, also including precipitation-type microstructures  [9,24–26] , are representative of HSs. Upon straining, the microscopic hetero-deformation surely occurs at the phase/grain boundaries still as a result of large mechanical mismatch among various phases. The hetero-deformation-induced hardening has been evidenced to play a crucial role in additional strain hardening for large ductility  [24–26] . However, these HSs are usually coarse-grained where the traditional dislocation plasticity still dominates.

The classical method to measure back stress was the Bauschinger tensile-compressive asymmetrically testing  [33,34] . Recently, a modified load-unload-reload tensile testing was developed  [35] . In addition, several physically based-models were proposed to measure the back stress  [36–43] . For example, the back stress relies on the number of Orowan loops and the radius of precipitates in the precipitation-hardening-type alloy  [44,45] . The back stress was twice shear modulus times eigenstrain in terms of the Eshelby's equivalent inclusion method which is suitable to particle- or fiber-reinforced composites  [46,47] . However, the microstructure-based model is scarce to directly calculate the back-stress.

In this study, both the hetero-deformation and resultant strengthening and hardening were investigated in detail during tensile deformation in a high specific strength dual-phase steel. The ductile γ-austenite was matrix, while hard and almost non-deformable FeAl-type B 2  intermetallic compound served as the second phase. The pioneering work by Kim et al.  [48]  exhibited a superior synergy of high yield strength of 1.2 GPa along with large ductility of ∼20%. Here, this steel was selected as a model material, because of large mechanical mismatch between two phases which makes it an ideal dual-phase microstructure to reveal the crucial role by hetero-deformation-induced strengthening and hardening. Moreover, the majority of γ-grains are, actually, ultrafine-grained with low initial mobile dislocations and weak tendency for dislocation propagations. This facilitates to further reveal the key effect of back stress-induced hardening.

sections.heading: Material, processing, and experimental methods
paragraphs:
The dual-phase (DP) steel was produced by arc melting in a high frequency induction furnace under pure argon atmosphere. The chemical composition was 16Mn, 10Al, 5Ni, 0.86C, balance Fe, all in weight percent.  Fig. 1 
                       illustrated the schematic processing route. First, the cylindrical ingot was cast of a diameter of 130 mm and length of 200 mm and homogenized at 1180 °C for 2 h. The ingot was then hot-forged at 1050 °C into slabs of 14 mm-thick, hot-rolled at starting temperature of 1050 °C into strips of 7.3 mm-thick, and cold-rolled to sheets of 1 mm-thick. The final partial recrystallization annealing was conducted at 900 °C for 3 min immediately followed by water quenching.

Both the monotonic and interrupted load-unload-reload (LUR) tensile testing were performed at a quasi-static strain rate of 5 × 10 −4  s −1  and room temperature by using an MTS Landmark testing machine. The dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens were cut from the annealed sheet with longitudinal axes parallel to rolling direction. The cross-sectional area was 4 × 1 mm 2  and gauge length was 20 mm. During LUR testing, the tensile specimen was stretched at first to certain strain under the strain control mode, then unloaded under stress control mode, and finally reloaded to the next unloading strain under strain control mode. The extensometer was attached to measure tensile strains during the whole tensile deformation. Three tensile tests were conducted for reproductive results.

The microstructural characterization was performed by using electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD, JSM-7001F) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-2100). Both the Schmid factor and Kernel average misorientation (KAM) values were measured  [49,50]  near both γ/γ grain boundaries and γ/B2 phase boundaries with respect to tensile strains, for the purpose of revealing the nature of hetero-deformation and strain hardening.

sections.heading: Yield-drop and hysteresis loop during tensile deformation
paragraphs: Both the yield-drop and hysteresis loop are experimentally evidenced to be two critical tensile responses in the DP microstructure. Particularly, both continuously take place during the whole uniform deformation.

The yield-drop, typical of yield-point phenomenon, is observed to happen at first soon after yielding, see  Fig. 3 a. To be specific, a yield-drop appears immediately followed by an up-turn of strain hardening rate, see insets A and B in  Fig. 3 a. Clearly, yield-drop is well consistent with that previously observed in other hetero-structures  [11,15 , 58,59] . The yield-drop results probably from the shortage of mobile dislocations during initial yielding in the DP microstructure, as seen in  Fig. 3 c. The dislocation source-limiting mechanism may be interpretive  [58] . It has been widely reported that the dislocation source is hard to activate in ultrafine-grains especially via the route of severe plastic deformation, even with annealing  [3,4,6,59] . Once dislocation sources get activated at elevated flow stress, the flow stress will decrease quickly after dislocation emissions  [58,59] . The yield-drop indicates, actually, an extra increase in yield strength. Later with continuous production of dislocations, the strain hardening rate shows, therefore, an up-turn (inset B in  Fig. 3 a), along with the recovery of intra-granular dislocation plasticity  [15,16] .

Of special note is the repeated presence of yield-drop after each reload, see  Fig. 3 e. This indicates the persistent shortage of mobile dislocations during tensile deformation. In other words, the traditional dislocation plasticity is not enough to sustain enough forest hardening for large ductility. Just in terms of the monotonic tensile curve ( Fig. 3 a), a simple conclusion is easily drawn that intra-granular dislocation plasticity and forest hardening reigns over the whole stage of uniform deformation. Yet, the present interrupted tensile test ( Figs. 3 b–e) just unmasks the nature behind hetero-deformation. The ceaseless presence of yield-drop is probably ascribed to lots of small γ-grains where both the production and multiplication of dislocations are not easy which makes the source-limiting mechanism operate all through uniform deformation.

The presence of hysteresis loops acts, in essence, as a critical sign for the operation of back stress during the hetero-deformation as is widely evidenced in hetero-structures  [11–15 , 35] . The back stress is derived mainly from incompatibility of varying kinds as a result of mechanical mismatch between two phases, e.g. yield strength and plastic deformability etc. This is the reason why hysteresis loop is observed to occur from the onset of yielding ( Fig. 3 b) straight to the ending of tensile deformation ( Fig. 3 c and d). The almost non-deformable B2 phase exerts strong constraint to plastic deformation of γ-grains through γ/B2 phase boundaries. As a result, back stress generates in ductile γ-grains, while forward stress is in B2 phase  [13] . Microstructurally, the back stress corelates to the introduction of GNDs, which induces both the strengthening and hardening as discussed in the following.

sections.heading: Hetero-deformation-induced strengthening
paragraphs: Yielding is, actually, typical of elasto-plastic co-deformation in the DP microstructure. This is due to the vast difference of yield strength between two phases. For example, the micro-hardness of B2 is 1235 Hv  [57] , nearly an order of magnitude larger than ∼175 Hv in γ. Upon yielding, soft γ-grains will start plastic deformation at first, while strong B2 phase still maintain elastic. This leads to the Poisson's ratio effect  [16] , i.e., mechanical incompati-bility between already deformed γ-grains and elastic B2, respectively, with Poisson's ratio of 0.5 and 0.3. Resultantly, B2 phase will exert strong constraint to plastic deformation in γ-grains. This produces strain gradient across γ/B2 phase boundaries. Therefore, the GNDs are generated at first inside γ-grains to provide compatible deformation. The increase in KAM values (see  Fig. 6 c) in γ-grains near B2 is the direct result for the GND formation.

Further, these GNDs will be blocked by and pile up against γ/B2 phase boundaries  [11–13] . This produces inter-granular back stresses  [11–13,30] . The back stress is directional and offset part of applied shear stress, which makes it difficult to further emit mobile dislocations from activated dislocation source  [13] . In other words, back stress renders the flow stress to elevate in γ-grains by the time the whole sample yields. Therefore, back stress will make γ-grains appear stronger to sustain higher applied stress. This is the reason that back stress induces an extra strengthening effect  [11,13] . Hence, the back stress-induced strengthening is, actually, inherent in HSs as a result of hetero-deformation. In addition, the aforesaid dislocation source-limiting mechanism induces also an elevated flow stress and contributes to a strengthening effect.

sections.heading: Hetero-deformation-induced hardening
paragraphs:
Strain hardening of two kinds operates simultaneously in the present DP microstructure, as illustrated in  Fig. 4 . One is back stress hardening associated with the accumulation of GNDs, while the other is forest hardening related to the statistically stored dislocations (SSDs)  [60] .  Fig. 4  demonstrates clearly the evolution of two hardening responses during plastic deformation. Strain hardening may be derived as  [13,14] :

The back stress-induced hardening is resulted from the production of GNDs. B2 phase, on the whole, only bears a small portion of plastic strains  [48,51] , as evidenced by hardly any change in the average Schmid factor after tensile deformation ( Fig. 5 ). Also note the continuing presence of plastic mismatch between γ and B2, as evidenced by the large change of Schmid factor in γ and just the opposite in B2 ( Fig. 5 ). As a result, plastic incompatibility exists steadily at γ/B2 phase boundaries in response to tensile deformation. This leads to the incessant generation of the GNDs to induce back stress.

The GNDs located mainly near phase boundaries for compatible deformation. Also note that these GNDs are, in principle, immovable  [28–30] . The interaction with newly-generated dislocations usually leads to a strong pinning effect, reducing mobility of these dislocation. With increasing tensile strains, on one hand, less and less room is left for small γ-grains to further accommodate more dislocations. This leads to hardly any mobile dislocations upon yielding when reload, as evidenced by the repeated and reinforced yield-drop ( Fig. 3 e). On the other hand, more GNDs, if possible, will be produced near boundaries for sustainable plastic deformation. Meanwhile, strain partitioning is inevitable between two phases. All these induce strain gradient and makes the continuous production of GNDs, as shown by an increment in KAM values especially in γ-grains bordering on B2 ( Figs. 6  and  7 ). Both the back stress and back stress-induced hardening will, therefore, play a growing role as tensile strain increases. The continuous presence of hysteresis loops of increased residual plastic strain ( Fig. 3 d) lends strong support that back stress hardening dominates.

Finally, it is further shown that over the entire tensile deformation, both back stress and back stress-induced hardening by experimental measurements are well consistent with those predicted in terms of the developed microstructure-based model in the present DP steel, as seen from  Fig. 9 a and b. Based on the model, the correlation of back stress with the key parameters in the dual-phase microstructure is well understood. For example, back stress will increase as B2 phase either increases the volume fraction or decreases the grain sizes. This is because both lead to an increase in the density of GNDs by increasing the number and degree for plastic incompatibility.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
The high specific strength steel, here, provides an opportunity to uncover deformation physics especially at ultra-high yield strength in dual-phase microstructure. Ductility of over 20% arouses interest to investigate strain hardening. Particularity lies in vast mismatch of mechanical responses between two phases upon applied loading, namely strong B2 inter-metallic compounds of absence of plasticity serving as the second phase in the matrix of ductile γ-austenite. Specifically, hetero-deformation makes both the back stress-induced strengthening and strain hardening as well prominent. The main results help to shed light on the path for understanding of the hetero-deformation-induced effect in dual-phase micro-structures. The main conclusions are drawn as follows. 
                         
                            (1) 
                            This DP microstructure yields in the form of typical elasto-plastic co-deformation due to vast mismatch of yield strength between γ- and B2-phase. Hysteresis loop appears during yielding, indicative of the operation of back stress related to the production of GNDs as evidenced by an increase in KAM values in γ-grains bordering on B2. Also, yield-drop followed by an up-turn of strain hardening rate occurs as a sign of the initial shortage of mobile dislocations. The strengthening effect is proposed by both the back stress-hardening and source-limiting mechanism, which leads to an increase in yield strength. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            During tensile deformation, the persistent presence of both hysteresis loop and yield-drop is visible during interrupted unload-reload cycle. It is further demonstrated that both the back stress and back stress-induced hardening account for, respectively, a large proportion of flow stress and global strain hardening. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            γ-grains, especially bordering on B2 phase, exhibit the large increment for both Schmid factor and KAM values during tensile deformation, as compared to the neglectable change of both in either B2-phase or γ-grains next to still γ grains. This indicates that these γ-grains bear a majority of applied plastic strains, together with main compatible deformation by the production of geometrically necessary dislocations of high density. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            The hetero-deformation-induced hardening, i.e. back-stress hardening is proposed. Vast plastic mismatch between two phases serves as the microstructural origin of back stress. In response to hetero-deformation, the geometrically necessary dislocations have to be formed to accommodate strain gradient. A microstructure-based model is developed to describe the back stress and the effect by dual-phase microstructure. The back stress predicted by the model is well consistent with the experimental result.
